entry.evidence: planktonic foraminifera should have responded to the rapid temperature rise that accompanied the end of the last ice age by habitat tracking

sequences.source_document: Strack et al. 2022, published article (XML text and PDF)

steps.action: Framed the gap: biodiversity monitoring spans about a century, and basin-scale fossil plankton records of the last deglaciation have not been used to study ecological change.
steps.quote: However, their potential to reveal the ecological changes of the planktonic communities on a basin-wide scale during the last climatic upheaval has never been exploited.

steps.action: Stated habitat tracking as the expected response, using cited premises (no late-Quaternary extinctions or originations, static thermal niches), and set against it a rival response involving processes beyond temperature-driven tracking.
steps.quote: planktonic foraminifera should have responded to the rapid temperature rise that accompanied the end of the last ice age by habitat tracking

steps.action: Derived the predictions verbally. Habitat tracking implies compositional change scaled to forcing and conserved assemblages. The rival implies change out of pace with forcing and possibly novel assemblages.
steps.quote: the fossil record should reveal an ecological response that was not always in pace with the environmental forcing, and potentially the emergence of novel assemblages

steps.action: Selected 25 North Atlantic assemblage time series from 198 published records using fixed criteria (full counts, 23 to 3 ka coverage, resolution better than 1.5 kyr), revised all age models to the PALMOD approach, harmonized taxonomy to 41 species, and built an updated LGM compilation of 1,083 samples (Methods §4.1).
steps.quote: Here we compile a coherent spatio-temporal dataset of 25 time series of planktonic foraminifera assemblage

steps.action: Computed pairwise Morisita-Horn dissimilarity for 1,840 samples and ran a PCA mapped to RGB (Methods §4.2). This showed three main assemblages and a systematic shift from cold to warm compositions, largest in the mid latitudes, with a Heinrich-event reversal at 15-17 ka.
steps.quote: Across the past 24 kyr, there was a systematic transformation of assemblage composition from colder towards warmer species compositions

steps.action: Compared per-site PC1 trends (interpolated to 0.5 kyr, LOESS fit; Methods §4.3) with the cited data-assimilated global mean surface temperature (Osman et al. 2021; §4.1 ¶2). Composition tracked temperature until about 11 ka, then kept changing at the same pace for about 6 kyr.
steps.quote: Then, assemblage change seemed to decouple from temperature, as the faunal change continued at the same pace for about 6 kyr

steps.action: Calculated species richness and the proportions of species gained and lost relative to the oldest sample, with linear-model slopes as rates (Methods §4.4). Gains outpaced losses; gains were highest in the mid latitudes and losses greatest in the tropics.
steps.quote: The gains and losses components of the species richness change reveal an asymmetry between local colonizations and extinctions

steps.action: Established no-analogue assemblages: nearest-LGM-analogue Morisita-Horn distances show mid-latitude assemblages diverging from all glacial assemblages from the Holocene onward, later also at about 60° N and 20° N (Figure 4).
steps.quote: led to the formation of new mid-latitude assemblages without analogues in the glacial ocean

steps.action: Tested the no-analogue result against a null threshold taken from within-LGM nearest non-self analogue distances (99th percentile 0.06). The threshold was also checked for 2nd- and 3rd-nearest analogues (Methods only, Extended Data Fig. 5).
steps.quote: are significantly higher than could be expected to happen by chance, pointing to changing assemblages with no LGM analogues

steps.action: Reconstructed the latitudinal diversity gradient per millennium from richness and Shannon diversity (LOESS; differences from each site's LGM mean, Methods §4.6). Showed mid-latitude gains and a tropical Shannon decline producing the present tropical diversity dip.
steps.quote: leading to the flattening of the LDG in the tropics and ultimately the development of the present-day tropical diversity dip

steps.action: Posed post hoc rivals for the continued Holocene change: restructured ecological interactions, other abiotic variables, or neutral drift.
steps.quote: could reflect the restructuring of ecological interactions, responses to other changing abiotic variables, and/or neutral drift

steps.action: Excluded neutral drift as the main control. Drift predicts change out of pace during the deglaciation and change during the stable pre-17 ka period; neither is observed.
steps.quote: if neutral drift were the main control on turnover, one would expect assemblage change to be out of pace with climate change during the deglaciation

steps.action: Added a further rival: asymmetric gains and losses during the forced transformation imply a very long (>10 kyr) lag to equilibrium, that is, extinction debt.
steps.quote: indicating a very long (>10 kyr) lag between temperature forcing and plankton response

steps.action: Excluded a long lag on two lines of evidence: no change in the stable 17-23 ka period despite climate change before 27 ka, and a rapid fauna response to the Heinrich-event cooling. Chose the parsimonious explanation over faster response times of cold assemblages.
steps.quote: our data show evidence against a lag in the response that is longer than the century-scale resolution of our time series

steps.action: Considered whether the auxiliary (global mean rather than local temperature as forcing) explains the Holocene mismatch. Judged that it may partly explain the mismatch but not the emergence of novel assemblages.
steps.quote: This might partly explain the discrepancy between global mean temperature and the overall planktonic foraminifera response in the current warm period

steps.action: Proposed other drivers (food availability, seasonality, stratification) and a shift from abiotic- to biotic-dominated species sorting, such as reorganized trophic interactions, as untested candidate explanations.
steps.quote: one explanation could be a shift in the causes of species sorting in the planktonic foraminifera assemblages from abiotic-dominated causes

steps.action: Rated interspecific competition less probable on the basis of a cited study finding no detectable competition within planktonic foraminifera.
steps.quote: Here we consider competition a less probable cause as no detectable evidence for interactions

steps.action: Kept the claim that novel mid-latitude assemblages formed through poleward migration plus asymmetric gains and losses and persisted for millennia rather than being transient. Also kept the claim that the present tropical diversity dip developed after about 11 ka (§3 ¶5).
steps.quote: we show that the compositional uniqueness of these assemblages persisted for millennia after the rapid deglacial warming

end.claim: North Atlantic planktonic foraminifera assemblages tracked deglacial warming but kept changing for about 6 kyr after global temperature stabilized, forming persistent mid-latitude no-analogue assemblages, so the response was not uniform habitat tracking.

decisive_move.sentence: Without comparing the stacked per-site PC1 trend with global mean surface temperature, the decoupling after 11 ka, and hence the claim of non-uniform tracking, would not exist.

gates.evidence: Action: the habitat-tracking framing (§1 ¶3) shaped the selection criteria for compiled records (§4.1 ¶1), but all data were collected earlier by others for palaeoclimate work. Claim: the assemblage trend could have stayed in pace with temperature (§1 ¶3 predictions), and the no-analogue result was tested against a null threshold (§4.5 ¶1). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen; the Holocene rivals are posed post hoc in the Discussion (§3 ¶1).

imports.item: Principal component analysis and LOESS regression
RGB mapping of dissimilarity PCs (Ferrier et al. 2007)
Species gains and losses metric (Antão et al. 2020)

novelty_claims.quote: However, their potential to reveal the ecological changes of the planktonic communities on a basin-wide scale during the last climatic upheaval has never been exploited.

limits: No peer-review file was supplied, although reviewers are named (p. 1880), so no review sequence is coded. Decoupling from temperature is read from Figure 2a,d (p. 1874) without a formal test (inference). PC1 explains only 20.4-65.3% of variance per site (§2 ¶2). No sensitivity tests are reported for age-model uncertainty, the choice of temperature reconstruction, local versus global forcing, LOESS settings, or the 2.5-23 ka restriction. Data are compiled from published records selected by stated criteria; the selection was not varied. The Holocene rivals (drift, long lag, competition) are posed after the data were seen and excluded by verbal argument or citation. Sub-claim statuses: no-analogue assemblages exceed a chance threshold (confirmed against a null control); neutral drift and long lag excluded (best_explanation, parsimony); cause of continued Holocene change (none, explicitly unresolved, §3 ¶4); tropical diversity dip developing after 11 ka (descriptive reconstruction, estimate without stated uncertainty). The Reporting Summary gives average resolution as 0.06 ka against 0.60 kyr in Methods, likely a typo (inference).

disagreements.target: Expectation that planktonic foraminifera respond to warming by habitat tracking, with assemblage change scaled to forcing (refs 42, 43)
disagreements.support: Holocene assemblage change continued at deglacial pace for about 6 kyr after global temperature stabilized, and no-analogue assemblages emerged.
disagreements.quote: planktonic foraminifera assemblages continued to change at the same pace as during the deglaciation after the transition to the current warm period ended

disagreements.target: Long, centuries-to-millennia lags in turnover shown for tree species and large mammals (Williams et al. 2021)
disagreements.support: No change occurred in the stable 17-23 ka interval despite earlier climate change, and the fauna responded rapidly to the Heinrich-event cooling.
disagreements.quote: our data show evidence against a lag in the response that is longer than the century-scale resolution of our time series

disagreements.target: Extinction debt payment as the fate of postglacial species surpluses (Jackson & Sax 2010)
disagreements.support: Mid-latitude gains persisted without delayed local extinctions, and the novel assemblages stayed distinct for millennia.
disagreements.quote: the postglacial surplus of species in the mid latitudes (Fig. 3) was not lost by delayed local extinctions in these regions
